extracted.intended_audience: advanced students and researchers in analytic/modern geometry (19th-century mathematical readership)
extracted.subtask_description: Theory and computational methods for poles, polar planes, polar reciprocal lines and surfaces with respect to a quadric (surface of second degree) director; includes definitions, theorems, special cases (cone, sphere, central director), and worked examples for constructing reciprocal surfaces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of polar plane (general quadric)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a surface of the second degree (general quadric) with equation (1) and a point P(x1,y1,z1), the polar plane of P with respect to that surface is the plane given by equation (2) (the explicit linear form obtained by eliminating the line through P intersecting the surface).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derivation: draw line through P meeting the surface in Q and Q' and eliminate coordinates; the resulting linear equation in x,y,z is the polar plane. The plane is called the polar plane of P and P the pole of that plane. The full expanded coefficients and intermediate expressions are given and may be used to compute the polar plane for any given quadric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polar plane for a cone (vertex at origin)
rubrics_metrics.description: When the director surface is a cone with vertex at the origin (C=C'=C''=E=0), the polar plane of any point passes through the vertex; equation simplifies to (2').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because many terms vanish for a cone, the polar plane equation simplifies and always contains the cone's vertex; polar plane formulas (2') are provided for direct computation in this special case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polar plane of the origin (pole at origin)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the pole is at the origin (x1=y1=z1=0) the equation of the polar plane reduces to Cx + C'y + C''z + E = 0 (equation (2")).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the explicit polar plane formula when the pole is the origin; useful as a base case in computations and in deriving coordinates of centre and other simplifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Centre of a quadric and condition for polar plane at infinity
rubrics_metrics.description: The centre of a surface of the second degree is the point that bisects every chord through it; when the pole coincides with the centre PQ = PQ' so the polar plane of the centre is at infinity. The coordinates (t,u,v) of the centre satisfy the linear system (3) obtained by setting coefficients of x,y,z in the polar-plane equation to zero.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To find the centre, solve At + B''u + B'v + C = 0, B''t + A'u + Bv + C' = 0, B't + Bu + A''v + C'' = 0 (equations (3)). Substituting centre coordinates simplifies other polar formulae (see subsequent simplifications for N,N',N",D).

rubrics_metrics.name: Harmonic relation between intersections of line with quadric (PQ, PQ') and pole distances
rubrics_metrics.description: If a line through P meets the quadric in Q and Q' and PP' is the distance between pole and its conjugate harmonic point, then PQ and PQ' satisfy a harmonic relation: PP' is the harmonic mean of PQ and PQ' and PQ·? (quadratic relations) arise when eliminating in the line/quadric intersection (derived in text).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The elimination of the line–quadric intersection gives a quadratic whose roots are PQ and PQ'; properties of these roots (and the harmonic mean relation) underlie the polar-plane construction and are used in deriving formulae such as r being harmonic mean etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parallelism of polar planes for points on the same diameter
rubrics_metrics.description: Polar planes of all points lying on the same diameter of the quadric are parallel (equation (4) shows dependence on direction indices m,n only through the same linear form).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By assigning different coordinates along a diameter and inspecting equation (4), polar planes differ only by a constant term and hence are parallel; for cones the polar plane (4') is independent of pole coordinates along the straight line X=mz, Y=nz.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pole at infinity ↔ diametral plane (pole at infinity gives diametral plane)
rubrics_metrics.description: When the pole is at infinity (transversal remains parallel to a fixed direction), the polar plane becomes the diametral plane which bisects chords parallel to that direction; equation (6) gives the explicit diametral plane.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Take coordinates to infinity in equation (4) to obtain (6); for a sphere the diametral plane conjugate to any diameter is perpendicular to it, so polar plane is perpendicular to pole's diameter direction in that special case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contact/tangency relation: pole on surface ↔ polar plane tangent
rubrics_metrics.description: If the pole P lies on the surface, then the polar plane passes through its pole and becomes the tangent plane at that point. Conversely, if the polar plane passes through its pole, it is the tangent plane and the pole is the point of contact (see XVII–XVIII).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret geometrically: when pole moves to the surface, the enveloping cone with vertex at the pole expands into the tangent plane. Formulaic condition is given by the vanishing of the quadratic discriminant leading to equality in (1) and (2) — the tangent condition is explicitly described.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reciprocity of polar relation between two points (polar reciprocal points)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the polar plane of a point P passes through a second point R, then reciprocally the polar plane of R passes through P; such pairs are called polar reciprocal points with respect to the given surface (Theorem in XIX).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequence: the pole of any plane is the intersection of the polar planes of any three points in that plane. This reciprocity is used to define polar-reciprocal straight lines and surfaces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polar-reciprocal straight lines (cone case)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a cone with vertex O, if straight lines OP and OR are such that the polar plane of OP passes through OR, then reciprocally the polar plane of OR passes through OP; OP and OR are polar-reciprocal straight lines (XX).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This yields methods to compute polar lines and planes in the cone case and to obtain polar line of a plane passing through the vertex by intersecting polar planes of two lines in that plane.

rubrics_metrics.name: Locus of poles of planes passing through a straight line — construction of reciprocal polar line
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a straight line with parametric equations x = z m + p, y = z n + q (8), the locus of poles of all planes through this line is another straight line (the reciprocal polar); explicit elimination yields equations (9) giving that locus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set up plane coefficients so plane contains the given line, substitute polar-plane relations, and eliminate to get the pole locus. The derived linear system (9) describes the polar reciprocal line; special cases and simplifications are presented for coordinate planes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coordinates of the pole of a given plane — general elimination formula
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a plane ax + by + cz = 1 (10), formulas (11) (and following long expressions for N,N',N",D) allow computation of the coordinates (x',y',z') of its pole with respect to a general quadric by elimination and linear algebra.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text develops and simplifies N,N',N",D expressions (11–20) and gives practical simplifications when plane coincides with coordinate planes, and when the director is central or axes chosen along conjugate diameters. These provide an algorithmic recipe to compute pole coordinates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplifications using centre and special axes (central director)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the director is a central surface and origin chosen at its centre with axes along conjugate diameters, the pole-coordinate formulas simplify (see No. XXX, XXXI and simplifications around (12)–(20)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set centre coordinates and choose axes to reduce N,N',N",D; examples show very simple forms for poles of coordinate planes and simplified general pole formulas (20). This is recommended for practical computation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of polar-reciprocal surfaces (director surface concept)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two surfaces A and B are polar reciprocals with respect to a director surface C (a quadric) if points of A are poles of tangent planes of B (and reciprocally), equivalently A is the locus of the poles of tangent planes to B and B is the envelope of polar planes of points of A (XXIV).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the central definitional rubric: a correspondence between points and tangent planes across two surfaces mediated by a director quadric; corresponding points are poles/tangent-plane correspondents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tangent plane ↔ diametral plane relation for reciprocal surfaces (central director)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the director is central (e.g., ellipsoid, hyperboloid, sphere) and axes chosen suitably, any tangent plane to surface B at a point is parallel to the diametral plane of the director that is conjugate to the radius vector through the corresponding point of A (XXV).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the sphere case the diametral plane is perpendicular to its conjugate diameter, so tangent plane at B is cut perpendicularly by the radius vector to corresponding point of A; this gives geometric intuition and computational simplifications for spherical directors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spherical director: reciprocal proportionality of perpendicular to tangent plane and radius vectors
rubrics_metrics.description: When the director is a sphere of radius R, if r is the radius vector to a point P on A and p is the perpendicular from centre to the corresponding tangent plane of B at Q, then r·p (and symmetric relations) satisfy rp = R^2 (expressed as rp = R etc in text) — equivalently the perpendicular to a tangent plane is reciprocally proportional to the radius vector of the reciprocal surface in the same direction (XXVI).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This yields the convenient relation that in the spherical-director case the polar construction can be effected without explicit director: the polar construction reduces to relations between radius vectors and perpendicular distances; useful for constructing spherical-polar reciprocals and examples are given.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method to construct reciprocal surface from given surface using derivatives (general director)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given equation of surface B (u(x',y',z') = 0), the reciprocal surface A with respect to a quadric director can be found by equating the coefficients of the tangent plane to the polar-plane expressions (equations (3)) involving partial derivatives du'/dx', du'/dy', du'/dz' and eliminating x',y',z' using the tangent-plane equation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The general elimination procedure (No. XXVII) is stated and illustrated: compute partials of u, form the three linear relations (3), then eliminate x',y',z' via the point-on-surface condition to obtain equation of A. Simplifications occur when u is homogeneous (use Euler's homogeneous-function property to simplify (3')). Several worked examples follow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reciprocal of homogeneous forms and specific examples (ellipsoid ↔ ellipsoid)
rubrics_metrics.description: For homogeneous functions u of degree m, simplifications yield explicit reciprocal-surface equations; example: the reciprocal of an ellipsoid x'^2/a^2 + y'^2/b^2 + z'^2/c^2 = 1 (m=1 case) is another ellipsoid whose axes are reciprocally proportional to those of the given ellipsoid (example in XXX).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure: compute derivatives, apply formulae (5),(5'), and simplify — the text demonstrates the algebra leading to the reciprocal ellipsoid and notes applications (e.g., wave theory of light). Several other worked examples (paraboloid, paraboloid → quadric) illustrate variations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reciprocal surface of an envelope-of-planes representation (polar equation viewpoint)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a surface B is given as envelope of a family of planes parameterized by (l,m,n,v) with a relation f(l,m,n,v)=0 (and l,m,n direction cosines, v perpendicular distance), then the reciprocal surface A (with sphere as director) has polar equation f where v is taken to be the reciprocal of the radius vector and l,m,n its direction cosines (XXXI).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thus the law of motion of the variable plane (the relation among parameters) serves as the polar equation of the reciprocal surface; this is an effective construction method when a surface is given as an envelope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algorithm for poles of tangent planes to a developable (envelope) surface
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a developable surface as envelope of planes s = a + f(a)x + g(a)y + ... with parameter a and director a sphere, one may find the locus of poles of its tangent planes by substituting direction cosines and perpendicular distance values from the tangent-plane coefficients into the director-based polar relations (XXXIII and surrounding discussion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The method: express the moving plane's normals and perpendiculars in terms of parameters, set l = v x_i, m = v y_i, n = v z_i (from identification with polar plane when sphere is director), eliminate parameters to get locus of poles. The text indicates this procedure and works examples earlier in XXXI.
